[PATH:theoretical] Rodrik, D. (2011). The Globalization Paradox: Democracy and the Future of the World Economy. W.W. Norton. — Examines the tension between deep economic integration and domestic institutional capacity, providing a framework to test whether welfare losses occur when developing economies with strong institutions face large, strategically trading partners.

[PATH:literature] Acemoglu, D., & Robinson, J. A. (2012). Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty. Crown Business. — Provides historical and comparative evidence on how institutional quality and sectoral diversification mediate the welfare effects of trade, relevant to assessing negative outcomes under asymmetric market power.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank. (2020). World Development Report 2020: Trading for Development in the Age of Global Value Chains. — Empirically analyzes trade welfare for developing economies, including East Asian and Latin American cases post-2008, and can be re-examined to isolate effects of partner market dominance and strategic policies.

C006.subject: Free trade
C006.object: net welfare losses for developing economies due to increased exposure to external shocks and deindustrialization, even in those with robust institutional capacity and export-diversified sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade net welfare losses for developing economies due to increased exposure to external shocks and deindustrialization, even in those with robust institutional capacity and export-diversified sectors]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data analysis using the Penn World Tables and UNCTAD trade statistics to estimate the impact of trade liberalization episodes (post-1980) on manufacturing employment shares and output volatility in developing economies with high institutional quality and export diversification, controlling for global shocks. — Directly tests the deindustrialization and external shock channel by measuring sectoral shifts and volatility, leveraging the scope's specific conditions of institutional capacity and diversification.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of Mexico (post-NAFTA) and Vietnam (post-Doi Moi) focusing on firm-level and sectoral adjustment to trade liberalization, using firm registry data and input-output tables to trace welfare effects through employment, productivity, and exposure to commodity price shocks. — Provides granular evidence on whether net welfare losses occur despite robust institutions and export diversification, controlling for geographic and temporal scope.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review and meta-analysis of empirical studies on trade liberalization and welfare in developing economies, with a focus on studies that explicitly measure institutional quality and export diversification as moderators, per the scope. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess the net balance of findings under the specified conditions, identifying gaps and consistency across contexts.

scope.domain: developing economies with high institutional quality and diversified export sectors

qualifier.temporal: post-1980 period of accelerated trade liberalization
qualifier.geographic: developing economies in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Southeast Asia

C007.subject: Free trade liberalization
C007.object: long-term real per capita income growth in developing economies with weakly enforced competition policy and state-owned enterprise dominance
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade liberalization long-term real per capita income growth in developing economies with weakly enforced competition policy and state-owned enterprise dominance]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of tariff reduction episodes in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (post-1990), interacting with indices of competition policy stringency and state-owned enterprise share of GDP — Directly tests the conditional effect of trade liberalization on per capita income growth in the specified scope, using variation in enforcement and SOE dominance to identify the predicted negative relationship.

[PATH:literature] Rodrik, D. (2011). 'The Globalization Paradox' and subsequent empirical replications focusing on institutional complementarities between trade openness and domestic competition governance — Provides theoretical foundations and cross-country evidence that weak domestic competition institutions can turn trade liberalization into rent-seeking and productivity stagnation, consistent with the hypothesis' causal mechanism.

[PATH:empirical] Micro-level case studies of industry reallocation in Indian manufacturing after 1991 trade reforms, segmented by state-level competition enforcement and public sector presence — Offers granular, within-economy variation to isolate the channel: where SOEs dominate and antitrust is weak, liberalization may entrench incumbents rather than spur creative destruction, lowering long-run growth.

scope.domain: developing economies with weak competition enforcement and large state-owned enterprise sectors

C008.subject: Free trade

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade positive net welfare effects even for developing economies with weak institutions and concentrated commodity-dependent sectors]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel regressions using the IMF's Trade Integration dataset and World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI), focusing on Sub-Saharan African and Latin American economies from 1990-2020, with interaction terms for institutional quality and commodity export concentration. — Directly tests whether tariff reduction and trade openness correlate with welfare gains (e.g., GDP per capita, poverty reduction, or household consumption) in the specified scope, and whether those gains are moderated by weak institutions and commodity dependence.

[PATH:empirical] Case studies of trade liberalization episodes in Ghana (cocoa), Zambia (copper), and Bolivia (natural gas) using detailed micro-level household survey data (e.g., LSMS) and firm-level data pre- and post-liberalization. — Allows for causal identification of welfare effects in vulnerable, institutionally weak, commodity-dependent economies, capturing distributional impacts and net welfare changes that aggregate regressions might miss.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of trade under weak institutions and commodity dependence, e.g., extensions of the Melitz (2003) framework with endogenous institutional quality and Dutch disease mechanisms. — Provides formal conditions under which free trade might generate negative net welfare (e.g., due to rent-seeking, volatility, or deindustrialization) versus positive welfare, informing which empirical patterns would confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Country-level econometric studies of trade liberalization episodes (e.g., India 1991, Vietnam 2007) with panel data on sectoral employment, wages, and poverty indices, disaggregated by labor mobility measures (e.g., geographic migration costs, skill transferability). — Directly tests whether liberalization leads to net welfare losses in settings with high labor immobility and distributional conflicts, by measuring real income changes across affected sectors.

[PATH:theoretical] Computable general equilibrium (CGE) models calibrated to low-mobility economies, incorporating within-sector heterogeneity (e.g., formal vs. informal workers) and adjustment costs, to simulate welfare outcomes under alternative trade policy scenarios. — Allows controlled counterfactual analysis of how distributional conflicts and immobility interact to generate net losses, clarifying causal mechanisms that empirical data alone may confound.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of empirical literature on trade liberalization and welfare in developing countries (e.g., Harrison, McLaren, and others), focusing on studies that explicitly measure labor mobility constraints and distributional effects (e.g., Topalova on India, Kovak on Brazil). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess consistency of findings across contexts, identifying whether high immobility and sectoral conflicts consistently predict net welfare losses.

Princeton University Press. — Provides a theoretical framework distinguishing between institutional capacity and distributional conflicts as mediators of trade liberalization outcomes, offering testable predictions to compare against the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of empirical studies on trade liberalization and poverty/inequality in low- and middle-income countries (e.g., from the Journal of International Economics or Review of Economics and Statistics), specifically coding for institutional capacity vs. sectoral conflict proxies. — Aggregates existing evidence to assess whether the net welfare effects are systematically more influenced by institutional factors than by distributional features, thereby evaluating the hypothesis's dominance claim.
